claims.claim: The Acts of the Martyrdom of Cyprian is an anonymous, contemporary account of the last days of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, written in the manner of an official Roman court record.
The account describes Cyprian's return from exile at Curubis, where he had been sent by command of the proconsul Aspasius Paternus, and his stay in his gardens while expecting to be arrested.

Cyprian was taken to the estate of Sextus and brought before the proconsul Galerius Maximus; the text reproduces the interrogation, the sentence and the written decree, and ends with the order that he be executed by the sword.
The text is described as less a literary hagiography than an eyewitness legal record, and as one of the earliest and most reliable surviving accounts of a Christian martyrdom.

The work opens with an earlier hearing in which the proconsul Paternus told Cyprian that the emperors Valerian and Gallienus had ordered those who do not follow the Roman religion to observe Roman ceremonies.
The work is catalogued as Clavis Patrum Latinorum 53 and as BHL 2037-2040; a critical edition by Herbert Musurillo appeared in Oxford Early Christian Texts (Clarendon Press, 1972), pp. 168-174.
One medieval manuscript witness of the Acta (BHL 2038e) is in Rouen, Bibliothèque patrimoniale Villon, MS 1379 (U. 42), folios 131v-132v, dated between 951 and 1050.
